summary: Defines the CHILDREN extension for IMAP4, which lets a client learn whether a mailbox has child mailboxes without issuing separate LIST commands for each one. The document title says Message Action Protocol, but the protocol is the Internet Message Access Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3348 lets a mail server tell a mail program which folders contain other folders. The server adds one of two attributes to the folders it lists, so the program can show a sign next to the folders that need expanding without asking about each one separately. The server's answer is only a hint, because computing it can be expensive and the folder tree can change while it looks.

subtitle: Two IMAP LIST attributes that tell a mail client whether a mailbox has child mailboxes

tldr.problem: A mail client that draws a folder tree with a sign next to the folders that contain other folders needs to know which mailboxes have children. Without help from the server it had to send a separate LIST command for every mailbox it had seen.
tldr.mechanism: A server that supports the extension advertises the CHILDREN keyword in its CAPABILITY response and may mark each mailbox in a LIST response with the \HasChildren or \HasNoChildren attribute.
tldr.outcome: The client learns the answer from a LIST it was making anyway, although the attribute is only a hint because the server may be unable to compute it cheaply. The document records the behaviour as Informational and expected a more general IMAP LIST Extension to take the idea onto the standards track.

facts.label: Attribute form
facts.value: Flag extensions to the IMAP4 mailbox_list response

today: RFC 3348 is an Informational memo published in July 2002, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document expected a more general IMAP LIST Extension to take the idea onto the standards track, and left itself as a record of the behaviour that several vendors had already implemented.

sections.title: Why the Extension Exists
sections.content:
Many IMAP4 clients present the user with a hierarchical view of the mailboxes the user can reach. Rather than showing the whole hierarchy at once, it is often better to show a collapsed outline, especially when there are many mailboxes. It is common to put a visual clue such as a plus sign next to a mailbox that has child mailboxes, and to expand the hierarchy when the user clicks the clue.

To draw that clue the client has to know which mailboxes have children. Without this extension it would issue a LIST "" * or a LIST "" % for each mailbox. The document records that several IMAP vendors implemented the proposal, and that it is published as an Informational RFC rather than a standard.

The authors also expected a more general IMAP LIST Extension draft to proceed on the standards track, with similar functionality to the two flags incorporated into it, leaving this proposal at informational status. In that design a client could ask whether the server should return the information, which helps servers where computing it is expensive, because the server would only need to compute it for clients that can use it.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail program can show a list of folders with a small sign next to the ones that contain other folders. To draw that sign it has to know which folders have children, and without this extension it must ask about every folder separately.

sections.title: Requirements and the Two Attributes
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension MUST list the keyword CHILDREN in its CAPABILITY response. It MAY then return two new attributes within a LIST response.

  • \HasChildren means the mailbox has child mailboxes.
  • \HasNoChildren means the mailbox has no child mailboxes that are accessible to the currently authenticated user.

A server SHOULD NOT return \HasChildren when child mailboxes exist but none will be shown to the current user, for example because the client has no permission to access them. In that case \HasNoChildren SHOULD be used. If the mailbox also has the \Noinferiors attribute, the \HasNoChildren attribute is redundant and SHOULD be omitted.

A server may not be able to compute efficiently whether the user has access to all child mailboxes, and several users may be changing the mailbox hierarchy at the same time, so a client MUST be prepared to accept \HasChildren as a hint. A mailbox MAY be flagged with it and still show no children in a later LIST response. A server that cannot determine the answer MAY exclude both attributes, so a client cannot make any assumption about whether a mailbox has children from the absence of one attribute. It is an error to return both \HasChildren and \HasNoChildren in one LIST response, and an error to return both \HasChildren and \NoInferiors.

Two further cases are called out. The attributes might not be returned in an LSUB response, because many servers maintain a simple mailbox subscription list that is not updated when the underlying mailbox structure changes, so a client MUST NOT assume that hierarchy information is kept in the subscription list. RLIST, a command defined in RFC 2193, includes in its response mailboxes that are accessible only via referral, so a mailbox whose children are reachable only that way appears as \HasNoChildren in a LIST response and as \HasChildren in an RLIST response.
sections.plainLanguage: The server may put one of two attributes on each folder it lists. The client must treat that attribute as a hint, because the server may not be able to work out the answer cheaply, or may answer while folders are changing.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The two attributes are defined as flag extensions to the IMAP4 mailbox_list response, using the augmented Backus-Naur Form:

HasChildren = "\HasChildren"

HasNoChildren = "\HasNoChildren"

The document also warns that \HasNoChildren must not be confused with the IMAP4 attribute \Noinferiors, which indicates that no child mailboxes exist now and none can be created in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The two attributes are written as \HasChildren and \HasNoChildren. The second is not the same as the older \Noinferiors attribute, which promises that no child folder will ever exist.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension gives a client a more efficient way of finding out whether a mailbox has children. If a mailbox has children but the currently authenticated user has access to none of them, the server SHOULD respond with \HasNoChildren.

In many cases a server cannot efficiently compute whether a user has access to all child mailboxes. A server that answers \HasChildren when the authenticated user in fact has access to no child mailbox may convey more information about the mailbox than intended. A server designed with that level of security in mind SHOULD NOT attach the \HasChildren attribute to a mailbox unless it is certain that the user has access to at least one of the child mailboxes.
sections.plainLanguage: Answering the question can reveal a little about the mail server's folders. A server that cares about this should only say a folder has children when the signed-in user can really open at least one of them.

viz.caption: The example LIST exchange from the RFC

data.title: A server with four mailboxes
data.code:
C: A001 LIST "" *
S: * LIST (\HasNoChildren) "/" INBOX
S: * LIST (\HasChildren) "/" ITEM_1
S: * LIST (\HasNoChildren) "/" ITEM_1/ITEM_1A
S: * LIST (\HasChildren) "/" ITEM_2
S: A001 OK LIST Completed
